About: Gauss's Law — Flux and the Surface

Source

Topic
Electrostatics — Gauss's law
Concept
Flux through a closed surface depends only on the enclosed charge — never on the surface's size, shape, or where inside the charge sits.
Serves
Reading Φ = Q_enc/ε₀ operationally; distinguishing flux from field strength.
Misconception
"A bigger surface catches more flux"; "a charge just outside still contributes a little."

Guided Inquiry

1 · The scene

A point charge sits inside a spherical Gaussian surface. Field lines radiate outward and every line that crosses the surface is counted — outward as +, inward as −. The running total is the electric flux Φ.

Below, watch the two numbers: Φ (total flux) and E at the wall (field strength on the surface).

2 · Predict — double the radius

The charge is inside. You are about to double the surface radius R from 0.1 m to 0.2 m. What happens to the flux Φ?

3 · Observe

Drag the R slider from 0.1 m all the way to 0.5 m. Watch the two readouts closely.

Φ does not budge. E at the wall drops to a quarter, then a ninth, then a twenty-fifth — but the same field lines cross the surface, so the flux is the same.

4 · Predict — the charge outside

The charge is now moved outside the surface. Its field still reaches every point of the surface, and field lines still pass right through it. What is the total flux Φ through the surface?

5 · Resolve

Slide the charge across the surface wall. Watch the flux snap to zero the instant Q_enc becomes zero — even though the field lines continue to pass right through the surface.

That is Gauss's law in one sentence: Φ = Q_enc/ε₀. Not the size, not where inside the charge sits — only what is enclosed. The surface here stays a sphere, but the law fixes Φ for any closed shape you could draw around the same charge.

01

At a glance

A point charge sits near a closed outline, the Gaussian surface. The sim draws field lines from the charge, counts those that cross the outline, and reads out the electric flux Φ and the field E at the wall.

What you'll learn

  • What electric flux through a closed surface means.
  • How the flux is counted, with a sign.
  • What the flux depends on, and what it does not.
  • How flux differs from the field strength at one point.
The charge sits on the horizontal line through the centre, a distance d from it.

What's on screen

  • The charge, labelled q, and 24 field lines drawn from it.
  • The Gaussian surface, a teal circle labelled with its radius R.
  • A counter for lines leaving and entering, and a status line.
  • Readouts: Φ in N·m²/C and E at the wall in N/C.
See itLook at the scene as it opens. Watch for: a red + charge at the centre of a teal circle, with lines running out through the circle.

03

Flux counts the field that crosses a closed surface, outward as plus

Cut a small patch dA out of the surface. Only the part of E perpendicular to the patch passes through it. Adding that up over the whole closed surface gives the electric flux:

Φ = ∮ E·dA
The vector dA points outward. Φ is in N·m²/C.
  • Field out of the surface counts as plus. Field into it counts as minus.
  • The counter in the sim does this with the 24 drawn lines: lines leaving, minus lines entering, gives the net.
  • For a uniform field E at right angles to a flat area A, the flux is just E·A.

The second readout is a different thing. E at the wall is the field of the charge at the nearest point on the surface, E = k|q| / (R − |d|)². It is one number at one place. Φ is a total over the whole surface.

See itSwitch the charge to −5 nC. Watch for: the lines now pointing inward, and the flux readout turning negative at −564.70.
04

The flux around a point charge does not depend on the radius

Put the charge at the centre, d = 0. By symmetry the field is radial and has the same size E(R) everywhere on the sphere, so it is perpendicular to every patch. Then Φ = E·A with A = 4πR²:

Φ = E(R) · 4πR² = (q / 4πε0R²) · 4πR² = q / ε0
The R² in the field cancels the R² in the area.
q = 5 nC, d = 0E at the wallarea 4πR²Φ
R = 0.10 m4493.78 N/C0.1257 m²564.70
R = 0.20 m1123.44 N/C0.5027 m²564.70
R = 0.50 m179.75 N/C3.1416 m²564.70

Doubling R makes the field a quarter as strong and the area four times as big. Going to R = 0.50 m makes the field 25 times weaker and the area 25 times bigger. The same 24 lines cross the surface every time.

See itLet R grow from 0.10 m to 0.50 m. Watch for: E at the wall falling from 4493.78 to 179.75 N/C while Φ stays at 564.70.
05

Gauss's law: the flux is the enclosed charge over ε0

The result q/ε0 is not special to the centre. For any closed surface:

Φ = ∮ E·dA = Qenc / ε0
Qenc is the net charge inside the surface.
  • Φ is proportional to q. Each nC gives 112.94 N·m²/C, so 15 nC gives 1694.11 and −5 nC gives −564.70.
  • Moving the charge inside the surface does not change Φ. The field at each patch changes, but the total does not.
  • What does change is E at the wall. With d = 0.05 m and R = 0.10 m the nearest wall point is 0.05 m away, so E there is 17975.10 N/C, four times the centred value.

The sim draws only spheres. Gauss's law still holds for a cube, an egg, or any other closed shape around the same charge.

See itMove the charge to d = 0.05 m, still inside. Watch for: E at the wall jumping to 17975.10 N/C while Φ stays at 564.70.
06

A charge outside the surface gives zero flux

Move the charge outside and Qenc = 0, so Φ = 0. The field has not gone away. Field lines still cross the surface. But each line that enters also leaves, so the plus and minus crossings cancel.

q = 5 nC, R = 0.1 mlines out / inΦE at wall
d = 0.09 (inside)24 / 0564.70449378
d = 0.11 (outside)9 / 90.00449378
d = 0.303 / 30.001123.44

Distances d are in metres, E in N/C. The wall field is the same on both sides of the wall at 0.09 m and 0.11 m, because the nearest wall point is 0.01 m away either way. The flux is not: it drops from 564.70 to 0 the moment the charge leaves. Farther out, fewer lines meet the circle, but they still come in pairs.

Charges outside do add to E at every point on the surface. They just add nothing to the total flux.

See itSlide the charge from d = 0.09 m to 0.11 m. Watch for: Φ dropping from 564.70 to 0.00 while the counter shows 9 leaving and 9 entering.
07

Where it matters

  • Symmetric charges. When the charge has spherical, cylindrical or planar symmetry, you pick a surface where E is constant and perpendicular. Then Φ = E·A and Gauss's law gives E directly. This is how the field of a charged sphere, a long wire and a sheet are found.
  • Conductors. Inside the metal of a conductor at rest, E = 0, so a surface drawn just inside it encloses no net charge. Any excess charge sits on the outside surface.
  • A law for all fields. Gauss's law is one of Maxwell's four equations. It holds whether or not the charge is symmetric, but it is only easy to use as a shortcut when the symmetry is there.
  • Careful. Φ depends only on the enclosed charge, but E in the integral is the field of all charges.
08

Summary

In one line. The flux through a closed surface counts the field crossing it, outward as plus. The sim lets you test what that total depends on.

Key points

  • Φ = ∮E·dA is the net field crossing a closed surface.
  • Φ = Qenc / ε0: only the charge inside matters, not the radius and not where inside it sits.
  • A charge outside gives Φ = 0, since every line that enters also leaves.
  • E at the wall is the field at one point. It changes with R and d while Φ does not.

Common mix-ups

  • "A bigger surface catches more flux." The area grows, but the field at the wall shrinks by the same factor.
  • "A charge just outside adds a little flux." It adds exactly zero.
  • "Zero flux means zero field." The field at the surface is still there. The crossings just cancel.

Things to try on your own

  • Set q = 0.5 nC and predict Φ before you read it. Check it against 112.94 per nC.
  • Put the charge at d = −0.05 m and compare E at the wall with d = +0.05 m.
  • Find the smallest R on the slider that encloses a charge at d = 0.30 m.
